mcqs.question: In a GraphQL API, a User type's orders field is resolved by calling an entirely separate Orders microservice, while its name field reads from a local cache. What makes this possible?
options: Each field has its own resolver function, so different fields on the same type can fetch their data from completely different sources
GraphQL requires every field on a type to come from the same underlying database
This only works if both services share the same database schema
The schema automatically routes all fields to the same backend service by default
mcqs.explanation: Resolvers are attached per field, not per type, so orders and name can independently fetch from wherever their data actually lives — a microservice, a cache, a database, anything. GraphQL doesn't require a shared database or shared schema between fields' data sources; that's precisely the flexibility resolvers provide.

mcqs.question: A query requests 50 users and each user's orders field. Without batching, how many backend calls does a naive resolver implementation make, and what fixes it?
options: 1 call total — GraphQL always batches automatically with no extra work
51 calls (1 for users + 50 for orders, one per user) — fixed by a DataLoader-style batching layer that combines the per-user calls into one
50 calls total, since the initial users fetch is free
It depends only on network latency, not on the number of separate calls made
mcqs.explanation: The naive path issues one call for the 50 users, then one more per user for their orders — 51 total. A DataLoader batches all the orders resolver calls queued in the same tick into a single IN-clause query, cutting 51 round trips down to about 2. Batching is not automatic by default; it has to be wired in, and the count is about call volume, not just latency.

mcqs.question: A public API is consumed almost entirely by third parties who all want the same fixed set of fields, and heavy CDN caching of GET responses is a major performance requirement. Based on the compare slide, which fits better?
options: GraphQL, since its flexibility is always the safer default for any API
REST, since GET-based endpoints cache easily by default, and the uniform, predictable field needs don't benefit much from client-specified shape
Neither — this scenario requires a custom binary protocol
GraphQL, because it makes CDN caching trivial for any query shape
mcqs.explanation: The compare slide notes REST's GET+URL caches easily by default, while GraphQL's typical single POST endpoint makes that kind of caching hard — and GraphQL's main advantage, client-specified shape, matters less when every consumer wants the same fixed fields anyway. This scenario matches REST's strengths, not a case for a custom protocol.

mcqs.question: A schema has users -> orders -> line items -> products, all nested relationships with per-parent resolvers. A client queries all four levels for 100 users with no batching in place. What's the risk?
options: None — since each individual resolver call is fast, the total query stays fast too
The call count can multiply at each nesting level, turning one query into potentially thousands of backend calls
GraphQL schemas cap nesting depth automatically, so this can't happen
This only affects response size, not the number of backend calls made
mcqs.explanation: Each unbatched level of nesting multiplies the call count by however many parent records exist at that level — 100 users could become 100 orders-calls, then far more line-item calls, then more still for products, compounding into potentially thousands of round trips. Per-call speed doesn't offset that volume, GraphQL doesn't cap nesting depth by default, and the issue is call count, not payload size.
